newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street stocks seen opening higher.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street stocks seen opening higher.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to open higher Thursday, following through on yesterday's rally.

However, analysts said any rise would be limited by nervousness over February jobs data due Friday. They said Wednesday's rally was fueled by relief after Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan eased fears that the Fed might be planning an interest rate hike.
"We're not out of the woods yet," said Peter Cardillo, director of research at Westfalia Investments.

"Of course, Greenspan made an effort to say his past comments were not intended to bring stock prices down," Cardillo said. "The next question, the really big question, is interest rates and will the Fed make any pre-emptive strikes."
He said the market would likeky have a higher opening as bonds and the S&P 500 Index futures contract were slightly higher, but he said any strength may be short-lived.

"I would not be surprised to see a reversal today as the market positions itself for tomorrow's employment report," Cardillo said. "If there are any substantial increases in wage pressure, the Fed could hike rates."
In Tokyo the Nikkei Average fell 232.18 points, or 1.27 percent, to 18,041.33.
In London the FTSE 100 Index rose 34.9 points to 4395.0.
Among U.S. shares traded in London, AT&T Corp was up 1/8 at 36-1/4. Chrysler Corp fell 1/8 to 31, Ford Motor Co was down 1/4 at 31-7/8, and General Motors Corp was off 1/8 to 57-1/8.
The dollar recouped early losses against the yen in Tokyo and was at a new 34-month high against the mark in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were thinly mixed, with the long bond unchanged to yield 6.83 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street column says small investors have long complained that they can be hurt when companies hold conference calls with analysts and big investors, giving the pros a chance to trade first on the news.
The column says a study being prepared for publication by three University of Michigan researchers suggests that the small investors may have a point.
The New York Times's Market Place column says although growth stocks have been lagging, analysts are keen on a new index, the Montgomery Securities Growth Stock index.
The index is based on 500 stocks for which Wall Street expects the greatest profit growth in coming years.
